item.title: Bayesian Unit-level Quantile Modeling with Application to Wealth Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.08843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modeling wealth quantiles over time and space and across fine-grained demographic classifications is of vital importance to policy makers. However, such data present unique challenges for standard small area estimation methodologies because they are highly skewed and heavy-tailed with both positive and negative values. Traditional area-level modeling and design-based approaches struggle to capture these features. Meanwhile, existing unit-level methodology frequently treats the survey design as ignorable and does not apply to surveys that are repeated over time. Often the analysis is restricted to alternative response variables that are non-negative, such as poverty indicators or income. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Bayesian, asymmetric Laplace pseudolikelihood model that is able to capture the major features of wealth while adjusting for survey weights and accounting for both spatial and temporal dependence. We present a Gibbs sampling algorithm for our model, as well as a variational Bayes algorithm for fast computation. We apply the method to the Survey of Income and Program Participation to characterize geographic, temporal, and demographic variation in the distribution of U.S. household wealth, including for sparsely sampled domains where direct estimates are unavailable or unstable.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Vedensky, Paul A. Parker, Scott H. Holan

item.title: Competitive Balance Beyond Standings: Bayesian Inference for Latent Tiers and Structural Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.08856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Competitive balance has long been a central concern in sports economics, tied to outcome uncertainty, fan engagement, and the way leagues design their policies. Most existing measures of competitive balance are built from standings or winning percentages, which say little about how overall parity relates to the way teams sort into latent competitive tiers. We propose a Bayesian framework based on the Bradley-Terry model that jointly estimates the number of competitive tiers and team memberships. To capture the overall degree of competitive heterogeneity, we introduce a structural balance parameter defined on the unit interval within a hierarchical model, and we establish theoretical results giving this parameter a clear interpretation:it is directly tied to the separation between tiers, and overall heterogeneity depends on both the size and frequency of cross-tier differences. Importantly, structural balance is distinct from the information content of the schedule itself, so leagues with different numbers of teams and games can be compared on equal footing. Inference is carried out with an efficient posterior sampling algorithm that jointly handles team abilities, tier structure, home advantage, and structural balance. Simulation studies validate the proposed method, showing accurate recovery of the latent competitive structure and correct performance of the structural-balance testing procedure. Applied to the NBA and NFL, it reveals that the two leagues exhibit similar global structural balance despite very different competitive organizations: the NBA has three latent tiers, while the NFL has two broader ones, and the NFL's sparser schedule produces considerably more posterior uncertainty. Overall parity, it turns out, can mask quite different forms of competitive stratification-something standings-based measures alone cannot detect.
item.dc:creator: Guanyu Hu

item.title: Supervised Factor-Augmented Matrix Regression with Weak Factors
item.description: arXiv:2611.08941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a supervised factor-augmented matrix regression framework for high-dimensional analysis with weak factors. When factor loadings are concentrated on unknown subsets of rows and columns, conventional full-matrix factor extraction may suffer substantial signal dilution, with weakness in one matrix dimension propagating to estimation in the other. We characterize this two-way weak-loading phenomenon for both \(\alpha\)-PCA and projected estimators and show that their loading and factor estimates may deteriorate under weak signals. To address this problem, we propose a sequential response-guided screening procedure that identifies informative rows and columns prior to factor extraction. We establish exact support recovery and show that post-screening factor re-estimation converts the weak-loading problem into a pervasive one relative to the retained dimensions, yielding sharper convergence rates under substantially weaker dimensional growth conditions and consistent factor-number determination. We further establish asymptotic distributions for both unrestricted and bilinear regression estimators based on the estimated matrix factors. Simulations demonstrate substantial improvements in support recovery and factor estimation under weak signals. We illustrate the gains obtained by the response-guided factor construction with two empirical applications.
item.dc:creator: Wenyan Hou, Zhaoxing Gao, Ruey S. Tsay

item.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data
item.description: arXiv:2611.09231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In permutation tests with discrete data, especially in small samples, different permutations often yield the same test statistic. The resulting ties can make the test conservative and reduce power. This conservatism can be particularly pronounced for maximum statistics: permutations may have the same maximum but differ at other endpoints, so the remaining endpoint statistics are discarded. We develop two power improvements for closed permutation maxT tests by refining the treatment of ties. The first method uses a single uniform random variable shared across all local tests in the closed testing procedure. This shared-uniform construction maximizes the rejection probability of every elementary hypothesis among all ways of coordinating the same randomized local tests. It also preserves an exact linear step-down shortcut. The second method is the deterministic two-endpoint augmentation (tea) test, which uses the second-largest endpoint statistic to resolve ties in the maximum. This additional information can favour rejection under alternatives while preserving null validity, without auxiliary randomization. Its full closure admits an exact quadratic shortcut. More generally, augmentation using any fixed number of endpoint statistics admits an exact polynomial shortcut. Both procedures retain every rejection made by classical closed maxT procedures and provide strong finite-sample control of the family-wise error rate under intersection-null permutation invariance. In simulations with sparse binary outcomes, both methods improve power over classical closed maxT testing. When many endpoints are tested, the tea test also often outperforms shared-uniform randomization.
item.dc:creator: Giovanni Corradini, Marvin N. Wright, Ronja Foraita, Livio Finos

item.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
item.description: arXiv:2611.09429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.
item.dc:creator: Ciarrah-Jane S Barry, Tahereh Gholipourshahraki, Zolt\'an Kutalik, Bjarni J Vilhj\'almsson, Esben Agerbo

item.title: Debias Online Expectile Regression for High-Dimensional Stream Data and Statistic Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.09431v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expectile regression is a powerful tool for capturing heterogeneous structures in data and has attracted increasing attention in large-scale data analysis due to its computational efficiency. However, statistical inference for high-dimensional online expectile regression remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose a debiased online expectile regression method for high-dimensional streaming data. The proposed method incorporates Lasso regularization to perform variable selection and alleviate estimation instability caused by high dimensionality. It further adopts an online updating strategy in which recursively updated cumulative statistics are used to approximate the global gradient, and a proximal gradient descent algorithm is employed to update model parameters. To enable valid inference when only the current batch and historical summary statistics are available, we also develop an online precision matrix estimation procedure. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed debiased estimator. Extensive numerical studies and real-data applications show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to the oracle and offline estimators while maintaining low storage cost.
item.dc:creator: Wei Cao, Shanshan Wang

item.title: A hybrid model for zero-inflated proportion data
item.description: arXiv:2611.09432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid model for analyzing zero-inflated proportion data by distinguishing two types of zeros. The first type arises from sampling variability, whereas the second reflects intrinsically unsuitable covariates. Accordingly, the hybrid model combines a regression component for suitable observations with an estimator of the suitability region that identifies unsuitable covariates. Using a debiasing technique, we establish the consistency of both the regression and classification components, together with the asymptotic normality of the regression coefficient and a convergence rate for the support estimator. Comprehensive simulation studies verify our theoretical findings. We further apply the model to two real datasets, where it outperforms most competing methods.
item.dc:creator: Yangzi Zheng, Qian Li, Binyan Jiang, Pinjun Dong

item.title: FlexRL: an R package for Flexible Record Linkage and Linked Data Quality Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2611.09439v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: FlexRL is an R package for probabilistic record linkage and inference on linked data. It provides a method to link observations from the same entities across two data sources that lack a unique identifier but share partially identifying variables. This method fits a hierarchical latent variable model of the data generation process, rather than classifying pairs of records from the comparison of their values, and accommodates registration errors and variables changing over time. Since linkage may affect subsequent analyses, the package also provides tools to assess the linked data quality as functions of the linkage decision rule. Two false discovery proportion estimators are implemented: a probabilistic approach contingent on the record linkage model and an augmented approach relying on an auxiliary estimation using synthetic data. Several measures of divergence of the linked sample from the source population are provided. These tools are agnostic to the underlying record linkage model and can be applied to any method. Together, they connect the output of the linkage to the validity of the subsequent analyses. The implementation combines standard R functions and S3 methods with Rcpp computations, resulting in fast execution times and a low memory footprint.
item.dc:creator: Kayan\'e Robach, Mark A. van de Wiel, Michel H. Hof

item.title: Scalable Estimation and Inference for Varying Coefficient Expectile Regression with Streaming Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.09484v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonparametric expectile regression methods face new challenges from streaming data, where retaining the full dataset for batch processing becomes increasingly impractical. In this paper, we develop a scalable nonparametric expectile regression framework for varying coefficient models. We estimate the coefficient functions online via functional stochastic gradient descent with Polyak--Ruppert averaging in a product reproducing kernel Hilbert space, requiring only gradient information and one pass over the data. For this online estimator, we establish non-asymptotic error bounds, prove its optimal nonparametric convergence rate under the proposed step-size schemes, and derive its Berry--Esseen bound for pointwise asymptotic normality. To perform online inference for the varying coefficient expectile regression models, we propose a multiplier bootstrap procedure that perturbs the stochastic gradients with independent random weights and recursively constructs bootstrap trajectories. We establish the bootstrap consistency of the online inference procedure, yielding asymptotically valid pointwise confidence intervals. Simulation studies and a real data application confirm the performance of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Haojie Dong, Xinyuan Song, Xinghui Wang

item.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2611.09539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a general M-estimation framework for censored regression models under endogeneity. A two-stage estimation is proposed to address the issue of endogeneity in the first stage and the issue of censoring in linear regression models in the second stage. The issue of endogeneity is addressed via instrumental variables using the control function approach. The issue of censoring in linear regression models is addressed via M-estimation using a suitably defined class of loss functions yielding a class of estimators. Thus, the proposed general M-estimation framework nests several existing estimators as special cases for the respective loss functions. Moreover, this provides flexibility of accommodating a broad range of robust loss functions that have not previously been studied in the context of censored regression. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the proposed class of estimators. An empirical study based on simulated datasets is conducted to illustrate general M-estimation for various choices of loss functions and to examine the finite-sample performance of various resulting estimators.
item.dc:creator: Swati Shukla, Subhra Sankar Dhar, Shalabh

item.title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses
item.description: arXiv:2611.09553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In clone-censor-weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term's effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5-6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0-4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.
item.dc:creator: Yuta Nonomiya

item.title: Local Inference for High-dimensional Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2611.09676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local stationarity provides a natural framework for time series whose dependence structure evolves smoothly over time. In high-dimensional settings, however, its classical definition can break down, as approximation errors accumulate across time-varying coefficients. To address this limitation, we introduce $(\epsilon_n,\delta)$-stationarity, a generalization of local stationarity that holds locally in time and allows approximation errors to grow with the dimension, and we combine it with local sparsity, which lets the set of relevant predictors change over time. We show that, for high-dimensional time-varying autoregressions, the rate of stationary approximation is driven by local sparsity, so that local sparsity governs not only estimation but also the stationary approximation itself. We then develop a \textit{local lasso} with time-varying penalties that selects relevant predictors and their periods of activity, and we derive error bounds that depend on the local sparsity, quantify the cost of nonstationarity, and guide penalty and bandwidth selection. For inference, we propose a desparsified local lasso based on local nodewise regressions and establish a linear representation with an explicit smoothing bias. Asymptotic normality then follows under two bandwidth conditions, one for coefficient variation and one for nonstationarity. Simulations and applications to macroeconomic and neuroscience data illustrate the methods.
item.dc:creator: Julien Bodelet, Davide La Vecchia, Johannes Lederer, Oliver Y. Ch\'en

item.title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2611.08541v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.
item.dc:creator: Shengxian Ding, Yifei Zhang, Xinyuan Tian, Yuanshuang Guo, Yize Zhao

item.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference
item.description: arXiv:2611.08560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over all estimators and over design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population of $\sum_i d_i$ potential outcomes, where $d_i$ is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit $i$. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are the potential outcomes, its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments, and its weights are induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class, and the unweighted hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential-outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes: joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory for average treatment effects without interference, saturation designs under partial interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.
item.dc:creator: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi

item.title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
item.description: arXiv:2611.08784v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Boris Landa, Francesco Strino, Fabio Parisi, Ruiqi Li, Yuval Kluger

item.title: Advection-aligned block Vecchia inference for spatio-temporal Gaussian processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vecchia approximations enable scalable likelihood-based inference for large Gaussian process models, but their accuracy depends on the choice of conditioning sets. For spatio-temporal processes with advection, target-centered conditioning can omit informative past observations. Motivated by total column ozone observations from the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS), we propose a data-driven, advection-aligned block Vecchia approximation that incorporates estimated transport direction into temporal conditioning geometry. Observation locations need not lie on a regular grid. An initial advection vector is estimated from the data and used once to select transport-aligned past-time conditioning blocks. The resulting graph is held fixed during optimization, while covariance and advection parameters remain free to vary. This separates neighbor selection from covariance estimation, avoids repeated parameter-dependent neighbor searches, and provides an interpretable connection between conditioning geometry and estimated transport. Batched graphics processing unit (GPU) operations evaluate the likelihood and its gradients. In a matched comparison of daily GEMS datasets from July 2024 and July 2025, advection-aligned conditioning attained a lower fitted Vecchia negative log-likelihood than target-centered conditioning on 53 of 61 days. In six Mat\'ern simulation scenarios with 120 matched eight-hour fields each, advection-aligned conditioning reduced advection-vector root mean squared error relative to target-centered conditioning at the same conditioning-block budget, with the largest reduction under strong transport.
item.dc:creator: Joonwon Lee, Michael L. Stein

item.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever
item.description: arXiv:2611.09214v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets---the data and code behind publications---in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal's reanalyses, years answering readers' questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal's reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit's hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record---confidential data included---without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.
item.dc:creator: Gary King, Yiqing Xu, Leo Yang Yang

item.title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions
item.description: arXiv:2611.09579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Loukrezis, Arthur Hatstatt, Bruno Sudret, Dimitris G. Giovanis

item.title: Calibrating demand models versus adjusting OD matrices with traffic counts: a controlled comparison
item.description: arXiv:2611.09678v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traffic counts are routinely used to calibrate travel demand models, particularly when the origin-destination (OD) matrix is not observed directly. An important modelling decision is whether to adjust individual OD flows or the parameters of the demand model that generates them. The latter approach uses fewer parameters and preserves a relationship between zonal characteristics and demand, but its accuracy depends on the assumed model structure. We compare three established approaches using the same prior information, traffic counts and equilibrium assignment. They estimate five production-gravity coefficients, origin and destination adjustment factors, or individual OD flows. Synthetic experiments on the Eastern Massachusetts and Chicago Sketch networks allow recovery to be assessed against known demand under different forms of model misspecification. Calibrating the five-coefficient model gives better OD recovery and held-out link-flow prediction when demand follows its assumptions or a two-purpose gravity process. Its advantage declines or reverses when destination choice or production relationships vary across zones. Cellwise adjustment achieves the closest fit to calibration counts in 65 of 66 evaluated conditions, yet it recovers OD demand least accurately of the three approaches in 45 of them. These findings show that model parameterisation matters beyond calibration fit. For transport planning, traffic counts should be used alongside independent evidence on trip production and distribution when selecting and validating a demand model.
item.dc:creator: Yue Li, Shujuan Chen, Ying Jin

item.title: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction
item.description: arXiv:2611.09698v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalized Bayes product partition models provide a probabilistic counterpart to loss-based clustering. They update a prior over partitions through an exponentiated clustering loss rather than a likelihood, so allocation uncertainty can be quantified without a full generative model for the data. However, their performance depends on the space in which the loss is evaluated. For high-dimensional observations, a squared Euclidean loss on the raw features can be dominated by irrelevant coordinates or fail to reflect cluster structure lying near a nonlinear low-dimensional manifold. We propose an extension in which an autoencoder and the partition are learned together, so that the space in which the clustering loss is evaluated is shaped by the clustering itself. Our generalized posterior combines a reconstruction loss, which keeps the low-dimensional representation faithful to the observed data, with a within-cluster sum of squares in the latent representation, which encourages cluster separation. Posterior computation alternates between Gibbs sampling over partitions and gradient-based updates of the autoencoder network, with the learning rate estimated jointly. We illustrate the approach through simulation studies and applications to four benchmark datasets.
item.dc:creator: Shen Jia, Weipeng Huang, Geng Yang, Eoin Gallagher, Tin Lok James Ng

item.title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.09790v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider Box-Cox transformations of correlation matrices, $\Phi_\alpha(C)=\mathrm{vecl}\{(C^{\alpha}-I)/\alpha\}$, with Jacobian $J_\alpha$. The family nests the raw correlations at $\alpha=1$, the generalised Fisher transformation (GFT), $C\mapsto\mathrm{vecl}(\log C)$, at $\alpha=0$, and the negated off-diagonal concentration coordinates at $\alpha=-1$. The inverse problem is a strictly convex program for every $\alpha$, so every member is injective. The map is onto $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d=n(n-1)/2$, if and only if $\alpha\le0$, such that $\alpha=0$ defines the boundary for unrestricted parametrizations. For $\alpha>0$ the image is bounded. The conditioning obeys the bound $\kappa(J_\alpha)\le\kappa(C)^{|1-\alpha|}$, where $\kappa(C)=\lambda_{\max}(C)/\lambda_{\min}(C)$, and on the surjective range the exponent is smallest at $\alpha=0$. Under Gaussian sampling with $n\geq3$, the asymptotic covariance of the transformed sample correlations is the identity at independence for every member, but only $\alpha=0$ retains the identity to first order in the correlations, whereas the leading joint third cumulant at independence vanishes only at $\alpha=1/3$. Finally, applying the transformation to the diagonal rescaling of $C$ that makes the result hollow adds a new family to the existing correlation parametrizations. For every $\alpha$ the rescaling solves a strictly convex problem and the inverse is explicit, and the scaled coordinates are unrestricted exactly when $\alpha=0$, where they recover the known global normal coordinates, centred at independence, for the efficient information metric of the correlations.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Archakov, Peter Reinhard Hansen

item.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.09792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.
item.dc:creator: Ayush Sawarni, Wenqian Xing, Tijana Zrnic, Ramesh Johari, Vasilis Syrgkanis

item.title: Optimal Forecast Reconciliation with Uncertainty Quantification
item.description: arXiv:2402.06480v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose to estimate the weight matrix used for forecast reconciliation as parameters in a general linear model in order to quantify its uncertainty. This implies that forecast reconciliation can be formulated as an orthogonal projection from the space of base-forecast errors into a coherent linear subspace. We use variance decomposition together with the Wishart distribution to derive the central estimator for the forecast-error covariance matrix. In addition, we prove that distance-reducing properties apply to the reconciled forecasts at all levels of the hierarchy as well as to the forecast-error covariance. A covariance matrix for the reconciliation weight matrix is derived, which leads to improved estimates of the forecast-error covariance matrix. We show how shrinkage can be introduced in the formulated model by imposing specific priors on the weight matrix and the forecast-error covariance matrix. The method is illustrated in a simulation study that shows consistent improvements in the log-score. Finally, standard errors for the weight matrix and the variance-separation formula are illustrated using a case study of forecasting electricity load in Sweden.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kloppenborg M{\o}ller, Peter Nystrup, Poul G. Hjorth, Henrik Madsen

item.title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series
item.description: arXiv:2412.03429v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Forecasting linearly constrained multiple time series, as those arising in National Accounts, energy systems and supply chain planning, requires that the forecasts of all variables jointly satisfy the underlying accounting or resource-balance identities. When several experts provide forecasts for some or all of the variables, classical forecast combination operates on each variable and ignores the linear constraints, while forecast reconciliation enforces such constraints by using a single forecast per variable. To bridge this gap, we develop an original coherent forecast combination framework, in which the joint problem of combination across experts and coherence across variables is formulated as a linearly constrained optimization problem. Closed-form expressions are derived for the coherent combined forecast and its error covariance matrix, and the statistical properties of the resulting estimators are discussed. A Monte Carlo experiment and a forecasting application to an Australian daily electricity generation dataset confirm that the proposed approach significantly improves forecast accuracy with respect to standard forecast combination and reconciliation alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Girolimetto, Tommaso Di Fonzo

item.title: postcard: An R Package for Marginal Effect Estimation with or without Prognostic Score Adjustment
item.description: arXiv:2510.13347v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Covariate adjustment is a widely used technique in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) for improving the efficiency of treatment effect estimators. By adjusting for predictive baseline covariates, variance can be reduced, enhancing statistical precision and study power. Rosenblum and van der Laan [2010] use the framework of generalized linear models (GLMs) in a plug-in analysis to show efficiency gains using covariate adjustment for marginal effect estimation. Recently the use of prognostic scores as adjustment covariates has gained popularity. Schuler et al. [2022] introduce and validate the method for continuous endpoints using linear models. Building on this work H{\o}jbjerre-Frandsen et al. [2025] extends the method proposed by Schuler et al. [2022] to be used in combination with the GLM plug-in procedure [Rosenblum and van der Laan, 2010]. This method achieves semi-parametric efficiency under assumptions of additive treatment effects on the link scale. Additionally, H{\o}jbjerre-Frandsen et al. [2025] provide a formula for power approximation which is valid even under model misspecification, enabling realistic sample size estimation. This article introduces an R package, which implements the GLM plug-in method with or without PrOgnoSTic CovARiate aDjustment, postcard. The package has two core features: (1) estimating marginal effects and the variance hereof (with or without prognostic adjustment) and (2) approximating statistical power. Functionalities also include integration of the Discrete Super Learner for constructing prognostic scores and simulation capabilities for exploring the methods in practice. Through examples and simulations, we demonstrate postcard as a practical toolkit for statisticians.
item.dc:creator: Mathias Lerbech Jeppesen, Emilie H{\o}jbjerre-Frandsen

item.title: Multi-layer dissolution exponential-family models for weighted signed networks
item.description: arXiv:2511.03420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding the structure of signed weighted networks is essential for analysing complex systems in which relationships between nodes vary both in sign and strength. Despite significant advances in statistical network analysis, there is still a lack of models that can account for both the sign and the strength of interactions in networks. We introduce a multi-layer dissolution exponential random graph modelling framework that enables systematic assessment of structural balance effects. We adopt a fully-probabilistic hierarchical approach that partially pools information across layers, with parameters estimated via an adaptive approximate exchange algorithm. A simulation study shows that the algorithm recovers the layer-specific parameters with small bias. We demonstrate the flexibility and explanatory power of the proposed methodology through an application to the gene interaction network associated with dilated cardiomyopathy, in which a multi-layer signed structure is constructed by progressively thresholding interaction confidence scores, with edge signs derived from pairwise co-expression. The analysis shows that positive co-expression edges embedded in positive triangles are more likely to persist at higher confidence levels, while negative edges whose endpoints share positive partners, which form unbalanced triangles, are preferentially dissolved as the confidence threshold increases.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Caimo, Paolo Dalena, Isabella Gollini

item.title: Conformalized Bayesian Inference, with Applications to Random Partition Models
item.description: arXiv:2511.05746v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian posterior distributions naturally represent parameter uncertainty informed by data. However, when the parameter space is complex, as in many nonparametric settings where it is infinite-dimensional or combinatorially large, standard summaries such as posterior means, credible intervals, or simple notions of multimodality are often unavailable, hindering interpretable posterior uncertainty quantification. We introduce Conformalized Bayesian Inference (CBI), a broadly applicable and computationally efficient framework for posterior inference on nonstandard parameter spaces. CBI yields a point estimate, a credible region with assumption-free posterior coverage guarantees, and a principled analysis of posterior multimodality, requiring only Monte Carlo samples from the posterior and a notion of discrepancy between parameters. The method builds a pseudo-density score for each parameter value, yielding a maximum-a-posteriori-like point estimate and a credible region derived from conformal prediction principles. The key conceptual step underlying this construction is the reinterpretation of posterior inference as prediction on the parameter space, with interesting connections to classical Bayesian point estimation and credible set constructions. A final density-based clustering step identifies representative posterior modes. We investigate a number of theoretical and methodological properties of CBI and demonstrate its practicality, scalability, and versatility in simulated and real data clustering applications with random partition models.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Bariletto, Nhat Ho, Alessandro Rinaldo

item.title: Exchangeable Gaussian Processes with application to epidemics
item.description: arXiv:2512.05227v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling collections of related epidemic trajectories using exchangeable Gaussian processes. The proposed formulation induces structured dependence across time-varying transmission processes through shared latent Gaussian process components, leading to interpretable pooling behaviour, variance decompositions and intra-class correlation parameters that quantify information sharing across populations. The framework accommodates both direct and indirect observation regimes, including noisy measurements of effective reproduction numbers, latent transmission models for Chikungunya outbreaks and age-structured epidemic systems driven by partially observed infection dynamics. We discuss connections with broader multi-output Gaussian process formulations, including coregionalisation and latent factor models, while emphasising the interpretation of the proposed approach as a functional random-effects framework for related temporal trajectories. A simulation study investigates the behaviour of the proposed models under varying cross-population dependence structures including dependent, weakly dependent and independent settings. Across several epidemic applications, the proposed models demonstrate strong predictive performance while providing interpretable insights into shared and population-specific transmission dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Lampros Bouranis, Petros Barmpounakis, Nikolaos Demiris, Konstantinos Kalogeropoulos

item.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model
item.description: arXiv:2512.24748v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for genuinely unbalanced dynamic network panel data models. We first study a baseline one-way fixed effect specification and then extend the framework to two-way fixed effects. The model accommodates contemporaneous and lagged network spillovers, temporal dependence, and a listing effect that operates when a unit first appears in the panel. For the baseline specification, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the QMLE, characterize the incidental-parameter bias, and propose a bias-corrected estimator. We further provide a consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix, to enable feasible inference. Under the two-way fixed effect extension, we derive the corresponding asymptotic distribution, bias correction, and covariance matrix estimator, accounting for the additional bias component induced by the time fixed effects. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators and inference procedure. An empirical application to Airbnb listings from New Zealand and New York City reveals region-specific patterns in spatial and temporal price transmission, highlighting the importance of modeling genuine unbalancedness in dynamic network settings.
item.dc:creator: Zhijian Wang, Tuo Liu andXingbai Xu

item.title: Assessment of evidence against homogeneity in exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots
item.description: arXiv:2602.06910v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots are constructed by displaying all subgroup treatment effects of interest against subgroup sample size, providing a useful overview of the observed treatment effect heterogeneity in a clinical trial. As in any exploratory subgroup analysis, however, the observed estimates suffer from small sample sizes and multiplicity issues. To facilitate more interpretable exploratory assessments, this paper introduces a computationally efficient method to generate homogeneity regions within exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots. Using the Doubly Robust (DR) learner, pseudo-outcomes are used to estimate subgroup effects and derive reference distributions, quantifying how surprising observed heterogeneity is under a homogeneous effects model. Explicit formulas are derived for the homogeneity region and different methods for calculation of the critical values are compared. The method is illustrated with a cardiovascular trial and evaluated via simulation, showing well-calibrated inference and improved performance over standard approaches using simple differences of observed group means.
item.dc:creator: Bj\"orn Bornkamp, Jiarui Lu, Frank Bretz

item.title: Dynamic Bayesian Predictive Stacking via Markovian Spatiotemporal Propagation
item.description: arXiv:2602.08544v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This manuscript develops computationally efficient online learning for multivariate spatiotemporal models. The proposed framework relies on matrix-variate Gaussian distributions, dynamic linear models, and Bayesian predictive stacking to efficiently share information across temporal data shards. The model facilitates effective information propagation over time while seamlessly integrating spatial components within a dynamic framework, building a Markovian dependence structure between datasets at successive time instants. This structure supports flexible, high-dimensional modeling of complex dependence patterns, as commonly found in spatiotemporal phenomena, where computational challenges arise rapidly with increasing dimensions. The proposed approach further manages exact inference through predictive stacking, enhancing robustness and interoperability. Combining sequential and parallel processing of temporal shards, each unit passes assimilated information forward and then back-smooths it to improve posterior estimation, incorporating all available information. This framework advances the scalability and adaptability of spatiotemporal modeling, making it suitable for dynamic, multivariate, and data-rich environments. Simulation experiments and an extracted data analysis from the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) help evaluate and illustrate the framework.
item.dc:creator: Luca Presicce, Sudipto Banerjee

item.title: Competing Risk Analysis in Cardiovascular Outcome Trials: A Simulation Comparison of Cox and Fine-Gray Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.16031v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cardiovascular outcome trials commonly face competing risks when non-CV death prevents observation of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). While Cox proportional hazards models treat competing events as independent censoring, Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models explicitly handle competing risks, targeting different estimands. This simulation study using bivariate copula models systematically varies competing event rates (0.5%-5% annually), treatment effects on competing events (50% reduction to 50% increase), and correlation structures to compare these approaches. At competing event rates typical of CV outcome trials (~1% annually), Cox and Fine-Gray produce nearly identical hazard ratio estimates regardless of correlation strength or treatment effect direction. Substantial divergence occurs only with high competing rates and directionally discordant treatment effects, though neither estimator provides unbiased estimates of true marginal hazard ratios under these conditions. In typical CV trial settings with low competing event rates, Cox models remain appropriate for primary analysis due to superior interpretability. Pre-specified Cox models should not be abandoned for competing risk methods. Importantly, Fine-Gray models do not constitute proper sensitivity analyses to Cox models per ICH E9(R1), as they target different estimands rather than testing assumptions. As supplementary analysis, cumulative incidence using Aalen-Johansen estimator can provide transparency about competing risk impact. Under high competing-risk scenarios, alternative approaches such as inverse probability of censoring weighting, multiple imputation, or inclusion of all-cause mortality in primary endpoints warrant consideration.
item.dc:creator: Tuo Wang, Yu Du

item.title: Sparse Probabilistic Richardson Extrapolation
item.description: arXiv:2604.02072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Almost every numerical task can be cast as extrapolation with respect to the fidelity or tolerance parameters of a consistent numerical method. This perspective enables probabilistic uncertainty quantification and optimal experimental design functionality to be deployed, and also unlocks the potential for the convergence of numerical methods to be accelerated. Recent work established Probabilistic Richardson Extrapolation as a proof-of-concept, demonstrating how parallel multi-fidelity simulation can be used to accelerate simulation from a whole-heart model. However, the number of simulations was required to increase super-exponentially in $d$, the number of tolerance parameters appearing in the numerical method. This paper develops a refined notion of 'extrapolation dimension', drastically reducing this simulation requirement when multiple tolerance parameters feature in the numerical method. Sparsity-exploiting methodology is developed that is simultaneously simpler and more powerful compared to earlier work, and this is accompanied by sharp theoretical guarantees and substantial empirical support.
item.dc:creator: Chris. J. Oates, Richard Howey, Toni Karvonen

item.title: Smooth Concordance Metrics for Survival Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.06411v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concordance indices are widely popular metrics for assessing the ability of predictive survival models to discriminate underlying risk levels. However, these statistics have also been criticized for using only the rank orderings of the model's predicted risk scores and being insensitive to important model features, such as the addition of strong predictor variables into the model. In this paper, we address these limitations by developing smooth concordance metrics that model the underlying risk discrimination probabilities as continuous functions of the predicted risk score differences, where the shapes of these functions are estimated from the observed data. As a result, these smooth concordance metrics assess model performance across the entire range of possible risk score differences, allowing one to identify specific scenarios where the candidate model performs especially well or better than other models. Simulations show that the proposed smooth concordance metrics provide more detailed information about risk discrimination performance and are much more sensitive to the addition of meaningful predictors. We apply these methods to compare predictive survival models for cancer recurrence.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Hartman, Grace Richards

item.title: What is the Long-Term Value of Reliability?
item.description: arXiv:2606.11526v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe Chronos LTV, a system to measure the long-term impact of delays and other service defects on key business metrics. We use Markov decision processes to model customer interactions over time, and formalize our target estimand as the marginal policy effect with respect to moving the average delay rate. Given this setup, we show that we can identify long-term effects under a sequential unconfoundedness assumption where delays are as good as random given observed order characteristics; and can estimate these effects using a simple covariate-balancing algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Chenyu Qiu, Xu Kuang, Inessa Liskovich, Ali Rauh, Stefan Wager

item.title: Anchors Away: Navigating Single-Arm Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR-SA)
item.description: arXiv:2606.20341v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unanchored indirect treatment comparisons using single-arm evidence are increasingly used in health technology assessment (HTA) when anchored comparisons of randomized evidence are not possible. Existing population-adjusted methods, including matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) and simulated treatment comparison (STC), are generally limited to pairwise analyses and typically estimate marginal effects in the comparator study population, which may differ from the decision-relevant target population. We propose multilevel unanchored meta-regression for single-arm indirect comparisons (ML-UMR-SA), a Bayesian outcome-regression framework for synthesizing individual patient data and aggregate data from single-arm evidence. ML-UMR-SA respecifies multilevel network meta-regression to pool absolute outcomes rather than relative treatment effects, jointly modeling individual- and aggregate-level data and linking aggregate outcomes through marginalization over study-specific covariate distributions, enabling estimation across multiple treatments, studies, and target populations. ML-UMR-SA distinguishes assumptions required to identify treatment effects from those required to transport results to target populations. Valid inference relies on strong and often unverifiable assumptions, particularly conditional constancy of absolute effects and cross-treatment identifying assumptions such as the shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA). These requirements are made explicit within a Bayesian modeling framework that facilitates sensitivity analyses. In simulations without unobserved confounding, ML-UMR-SA produced low bias and nominal coverage for comparator-population effects. Transportability to alternative populations depended critically on identifying assumptions, whereas incorporating subgroup information restored near-unbiased estimation and nominal coverage.
item.dc:creator: Conor Chandler, K. Jack Ishak

item.title: Response-guided knockoffs for prespecified directional FDR control in linear models
item.description: arXiv:2608.29083v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional false discovery rate (FDR) control limits the expected proportion of selected features that are unrelated to the response. Directional FDR extends this criterion to also account for incorrect sign estimates. In some applications, however, discoveries are sought only in a direction specified in advance. We therefore introduce the prespecified directional FDR, which counts as errors both null effects and effects opposite to the target direction in context of the fixed-design Gaussian linear model with unknown noise variance. A straightforward adaptation of the knockoff filter provides prespecified directional FDR control. To improve power, we develop the response-guided knockoff filter, which uses a noise-perturbed response to guide knockoff construction in favour of features likely to have the target sign, while retaining finite-sample prespecified directional FDR control. Notably, our improved filter maintains this guarantee with a sample size $n>p+2$ in contrast to standard constructions that require $n\geq2p$. Simulations across a range of settings demonstrate power gains of the response-guided knockoff filter. An application to HIV drug-resistance data illustrates improved recovery of externally annotated resistance-associated mutations.
item.dc:creator: Jack Freestone, Garth Tarr, Samuel Muller, Uri Keich

item.title: Robust and Sparse Group Dynamic Causal Modeling via Student-t Parametric Empirical Bayes and Nonlocal Priors
item.description: arXiv:2609.06379v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic causal modeling (DCM) estimates directed effective connectivity, while parametric empirical Bayes (PEB) supports group inference using subject-specific posterior summaries. Standard PEB relies on Gaussian models and continuous shrinkage, making it sensitive to atypical estimates and unable to distinguish negligible from nonzero effects. We develop a robust and sparse group-DCM extension combining a Student-$t$ likelihood with a spike-and-slab prior using a nonlocal product-moment (pMOM) slab. A normal--gamma representation of the Student-$t$ distribution yields weights that downweight atypical {whitened residual coordinates}. The pMOM slab vanishes at zero, sharpening coefficient selection and yielding inclusion probabilities. {We propagate first-level posterior uncertainty through block-covariance pre-whitening and use a multistart generalized expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm with conditional maximization for mode fitting, followed by parallel-tempering posterior integration for inclusion probabilities. A simulation study showed that Student-$t$ weighting supplied the main protection against contamination, while spike-and-slab regularization reduced fixed-threshold false selections. In an openly shared mixed-gambles fMRI application, we found mild heterogeneity, concentrated inclusion support on departures of all four diagonal self-inhibition scaling parameters from the SPM default, and close directional agreement with standard PEB implemented in Statistical Parametric Mapping.} Our framework therefore adds interpretable {whitened-coordinate} robustness diagnostics and sparse coefficient selection to hierarchical DCM while retaining first-level uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Godfred Arhin, Nilotpal Sanyal

item.title: Calibrated Order-Randomized Rosenblatt Tests
item.description: arXiv:2609.37477v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We test whether a multivariate vector X conforms to a specified distribution F, as in copula modelling and density forecasting. The Rosenblatt transform reduces this to testing uniformity, but its arbitrary coordinate ordering affects power under dependence. We study order randomization: transforming under many random orderings and merging evidence with dependence-robust rules. Reordering only redistributes the Mahalanobis signal energy, so one ordering is a lucky or unlucky draw, and pooling raises calibrated power. We compare against two order-invariant baselines, the chi-squared energy test and the symmetric-root test. With F known, the e-value average over orderings is at least as powerful as the symmetric-root test in every setting we ran, and as the chi-squared test on concentrated and fully diffuse departures. With Gaussian mean and covariance estimated, the classical conditional probability integral transform keeps each ordering's p-values exact and e-values valid, a parametric bootstrap calibrates the pooled tests, and the comparisons hold except for deficits of at most 0.02 against the symmetric-root test on single-coordinate departures. Validating a Gaussian risk model for nine currencies, the test flags Brexit, COVID and other episodes; it extends to any null with computable, simulable conditionals.
item.dc:creator: Mehrdad Pournaderi

item.title: Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.21837v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In prediction-powered inference, predictions supplement labeled outcomes to improve estimation. We combine a prediction-corrected score and an auxiliary moment in a generalized method of moments (GMM) criterion. The resulting estimator is first-order equivalent to the corresponding corrected-score root under regularity conditions, but the auxiliary penalty can change the finite-sample fit. In a multiparameter Gaussian linear model with low noise, retaining this penalty reduces risk relative to bounded scalar corrected-score roots. We then introduce covariance-calibrated prediction-powered inference (CC-PPI), which uses prediction scores from both samples to reweight the penalty. With a spectrally protected half-strength update, CC-PPI retains regular first-order efficiency and strictly reduces risk relative to uncalibrated full GMM in a Gaussian linear low-noise regime that tolerates some prediction error and in a structured multiparameter logistic model conditional on the existence of a finite pilot estimate. Targeted simulations isolate the gains from calibration and show that they can reverse as prediction error grows. Broader simulations and four applications evaluate point estimation and the coverage and width of full-refit bootstrap intervals for linear projections.
item.dc:creator: Siyuan Chen, Yang Bai, Huichen Zhu

item.title: Stay on the Manifold: Hierarchical Bayesian Trajectory-Family Transfer for Sparse-Target Reconstruction and Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2310.07801v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Where should reconstructions and new samples lie when a few observations reveal only fragments of a trajectory? We propose hierarchical Bayesian trajectory principal-manifold sampling (HB-TPM), which learns a family of smooth curves from ordered source tasks and adapts it to sparse targets. For unordered vectors, alternating progression assignments and coefficient updates estimate trajectory structure between and beyond the observed shots under the learned source family. Observation-aware extensions connect the trajectory prior to photon arrivals and image-encoded cardiac cycles. Our analysis characterizes the coefficient directions supplied by the prior and bounds sampling error conditional on curve recovery. Across 30 held-out vector tasks, HB-TPM reduces mean sliced-Wasserstein distance by 21.0-41.8% relative to a source-adapted VAE. Prior-strength and sampling ablations identify coefficient shrinkage as the main supported mechanism. On 100 simulated photon records, adaptation lowers mean relative trajectory RMSE by 50.2% versus target-only fitting and 23.6% versus source-mean prediction. Across three training seeds and five folds on 98 cardiac sequences, HB-TPM with latent-MSE training achieves the best mean reconstruction among the tested configurations. Together, the results demonstrate trajectory-family transfer for sparse-target reconstruction and trajectory-centered sampling when source and target tasks share comparable progression structure.
item.dc:creator: Elvis Han Cui, Yuhan Pan, Xin-Ya Zhang, Bingbin Li, Yanan Li, Donghui Wang, Weng Kee Wong

item.title: Using Multiple Outcomes to Adjust Standard Errors for Spatial Correlation
item.description: arXiv:2504.13295v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A researcher interested in a particular outcome variable often observes dozens of other outcomes for the same units. If these auxiliary outcomes exhibit the same cross-sectional correlation as the outcome of interest, they can be used to estimate that correlation directly. We develop a procedure that uses estimates of this form to adjust standard errors in a given regression problem for cross-sectional dependence. We show, theoretically and with simulations, that the resulting standard errors can be substantially more accurate. Re-analyzing nine papers, we find that the proposed correction can make a meaningful difference in practice.
item.dc:creator: Stefano DellaVigna, Guido Imbens, Woojin Kim, David M. Ritzwoller

item.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness
item.description: arXiv:2509.17228v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clinical notes contain rich patient information, such as diagnoses or medications, making them valuable for patient representation learning. Recent advances in large language models have further improved the ability to extract meaningful representations from clinical texts. However, clinical notes are often missing. For example, in our MIMIC-IV cohort, 35.15% of patients have no eligible discharge summaries. In such cases, representations can be learned from other modalities such as structured data, chest X-rays, or radiology reports. Yet the availability of these modalities is influenced by clinical decision-making and varies across patients, potentially producing modality missing-not-at-random (MMNAR) patterns. We propose a causal representation learning framework that leverages observed data and informative missingness in multimodal clinical records. It consists of: (1) an MMNAR-aware modality fusion component that integrates structured data, imaging, and text while conditioning on missingness patterns to capture patient health and clinician-driven assignment; (2) a modality reconstruction component with latent alignment to preserve modality information in the learned representation; and (3) a multitask outcome prediction model with a rectifier that corrects for residual bias from specific modality observation patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across MIMIC-IV and eICU show consistent gains over the strongest baselines, achieving relative AUC improvements of up to 4.3% for hospital readmission and 2.7% for ICU admission.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Liang, Ziwen Pan, Ruoxuan Xiong

item.title: CausalCompass: Evaluating the Robustness of Time-Series Causal Discovery in Misspecified Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2602.07915v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal discovery from time series is a fundamental task in machine learning. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by a reliance on untestable causal assumptions and by the lack of robustness-oriented evaluation in existing benchmarks. To address these challenges, we propose CausalCompass, a flexible and extensible benchmark framework designed to assess the robustness of time-series causal discovery (TSCD) methods under violations of modeling assumptions. To demonstrate the practical utility of CausalCompass, we conduct extensive benchmarking of representative TSCD algorithms across eight assumption-violation scenarios. Our experimental results indicate that no single method consistently attains optimal performance across all settings. Nevertheless, in most scenarios, the methods exhibiting superior overall performance are deep learning-based approaches. We further provide hyperparameter sensitivity analyses to deepen the understanding of these findings. We additionally conduct ablation experiments to explain the strong performance of deep learning-based methods under assumption violations. We also find that NTS-NOTEARS relies on standardized preprocessing in practice, performing poorly in the vanilla setting but exhibiting strong performance after standardization. Finally, our work aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of TSCD methods under assumption violations, thereby facilitating their broader adoption in real-world applications. The user-friendly implementation, documentation and datasets are available at https://github.com/huiyang-yi/CausalCompass.
item.dc:creator: Huiyang Yi, Xiaojian Shen, Yonggang Wu, Duxin Chen, He Wang, Wenwu Yu

item.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2605.05024v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hypergraphs model higher-order interactions, but realistic hypergraph generation remains difficult because incidence, hyperedge-size heterogeneity, and overlap structure are not faithfully captured by pairwise reductions. We propose \HEDGE, a generative model defined directly on relaxed incidence matrices via a structured stochastic diffusion. The forward process combines a hypergraph-specific two-sided heat operator with an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck component, preserving structure-aware noising near the data while yielding an explicit Gaussian terminal law. Conditional on an observed hypergraph, this forward process is linear-Gaussian, so conditional means, covariances, scores, and reverse-drift targets are available in closed form. We therefore learn a permutation-equivariant state-only reverse-drift field in incidence space by regressing onto exact conditional targets, and generate samples by simulating a learned reverse-time SDE from the Gaussian base law. We establish exactness in the ideal state-only setting together with finite-horizon stability guarantees, and empirically show improved hypergraph generation quality relative to strong baselines.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Nemeth

item.title: NeuroMAS: Multi-Agent Systems as Neural Networks with Joint Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.16757v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent language systems are often built as hand-designed workflows, where agents are assigned semantic roles and communication protocols are specified in advance. We propose NeuroMAS, a framework that treats a multi-agent language system as a trainable and scalable neural-network-like architecture with hidden textual intermediate signals. In NeuroMAS, language-agent nodes are role-free but structure-aware: the topology determines how information can flow, while reward-based training determines how nodes communicate, specialize, and coordinate. This formulation shifts multi-agent design from workflow engineering toward architecture design, where depth, width, connectivity, and growth protocol become scalable sources of capability. We provide a theoretical perspective showing why such modular text-valued computation can be parameter-efficient when tasks admit stable decompositions. Experiments show that NeuroMAS improves over both inference-time collaboration methods and trained baselines, and that its gains are not explained by trainable parameter count alone. We further find that organizational scaling is path-dependent: larger systems can fail when trained from scratch, but become stronger when grown progressively from smaller trained systems. These results suggest that learned multi-agent organization is a promising scaling axis for language-model reasoning and generation.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: The First Conference on Statistics and Trustworthy AI for Cross (X)-Domain Acceleration (STAI-X 2026)
item.dc:creator: Haoran Lu, Luyang Fang, Wenxuan Zhong, Ping Ma

item.title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators
item.description: arXiv:2605.17778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in high-dimensional linear regression by introducing and analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We consider both spiked and general covariance matrices. For the former, we establish that when the covariance has $s$ distinct spikes, $s$-step self-distillation achieves optimal prediction among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $s$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(s-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For general covariance matrices, we show that self-distillation approaches the optimal limiting prediction risk among continuous spectral shrinkage estimators as the number of distillation steps increases. We further develop a generalized cross-validation procedure for selecting the distillation parameters from data and establish an asymptotic oracle guarantee for the resulting estimator. We also study a federated approach where multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server seeks to aggregate them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results explain why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods.
item.dc:creator: Radu Lecoiu, Debarghya Mukherjee, Pragya Sur

item.title: Robust Ensemble Kalman Filtering Under Observation Noise Misspecification
item.description: arXiv:2605.26881v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address observation noise misspecification in Bayesian filtering of dynamical systems via generalised Bayesian inference. Mismatch in tail decay between the true data generating process and an assumed observation model, often indicated via outliers, can strongly impact Bayesian updates in Kalman filters and their ensemble approximations. Adjusting information processing in the analysis step by employing diffusion score matching achieves robustness while maintaining closed-form Gaussian updates and good uncertainty quantification. We provide theoretical properties of this novel Kalman filter in linear Gaussian state space systems covering conjugacy of the analysis step, robustness, covariance stability, and tuning. We extend the approach to non-linear signal dynamics by adapting ensemble Kalman filter variants. Simulation studies on 2D target tracking and the Lorenz-63 and 40D Lorenz-96 systems highlight a critical trade-off between robustness and stability in filtering.
item.dc:creator: Hans Reimann, Sebastian Reich

item.title: Closed-form fractional radial links for elliptical Mahalanobis discriminant analysis
item.description: arXiv:2607.06089v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study binary classification when the two classes are elliptical with a shared radial generator $g$. The log-likelihood ratio is then an additive function of the two squared Mahalanobis radii, with radial link $\varphi=\log g$. For Gaussian classes $\varphi$ is affine and the rule reduces to quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA); otherwise the Bayes link is not the identity. Instead of fitting this link with a spline smoother, we derive its family from the within-class law of the radius and estimate a finite fractional-power projection. We prove that the link is identifiable from the radius law, that the plug-in estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal under finite-moment conditions, and that the induced classifier is asymptotically Bayes-optimal in an iterated sieve limit. For $d\ge2$ and non-nested class parameters, the identity link suffices only for affine (Gaussian) generators. The bridge, GAM membership and the affine direction of this dichotomy are verified in Lean 4. We compare against the global Mahalanobis-GAM of Ghosh et al. (2025), re-implemented with mgcv REML splines at equal input budget. On two UCI benchmarks the derived link ties with the fitted GAM. On six financial series from three asset classes, with validation that respects temporal dependence, it is never significantly worse than the fitted GAM: better on CAD/USD and tied on the other five. It beats QDA on the three heaviest-tailed series (oil $[+0.023,+0.069]$, S&P 500 $[+0.039,+0.125]$, JPY/USD $[+0.009,+0.047]$) and ties elsewhere. A rate simulation with a closed-form ground truth reproduces the $\sqrt{n}$ rate and, under covariance heterogeneity, QDA's risk floor against the derived link's vanishing excess risk.
